name: r3-surprises-1
statement: The cued base's deficit at T 1.0 comes from tail sampling: at every position there is a small chance of drawing a low-probability token that derails a step (slip, misread), and these errors add up with length; RL's diffuse change shrinks that tail at every position (so RL barely notices temperature), whereas any label-free way of cutting the tail (lower T, top-p, min-p, length cutoffs) also removes the tail tokens that break the base out of its self-reinforcing repeats, so loops come back and the net gain is about zero.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B with the 3-token cue against Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math, plain prompt, on MATH-500 and the clean hard328 set, one sample, cap 16,384, grader v3, T between 0.6 and 1.5 with or without top-p/min-p truncation. It covers per-token error rates, entropy, and accuracy as functions of temperature and truncation. It does not cover the Code pair, other model families, or why a = 0.25 of the weight difference already saturates (listed under conflicts), and it says nothing about the 16 cap hits without a loop, which come from failing to stop, not from slips.

imports.finding: Truncation samplers help only once temperature has already collapsed accuracy (largest gain +3.3 points on robust models). In fragile models the collapse shows up as outputs that hit the limit or never state an answer, and on those models truncation recovers to within 6 points of the T 0.7 level.
imports.how: This sorts the two models: RL has a shrunk tail, so it is 'robust' and temperature-flat. The cued base is fragile: at high T its tail mass shows up as derailed tokens, and cutting the tail moves it back toward the loop regime. So truncation has nothing to gain at T 1.0, where the base has not collapsed, and the theory predicts a collapse once the base goes above T 1.0 without truncation.

imports.finding: A selection-noise null predicts more than 75 % of the lift of the best random perturbation, and at K = 50 random weight search cannot be told apart from a majority vote over unperturbed samples.
imports.how: A matched-norm random weight change does not shrink the tail, so it acts as one more independent draw of the slip process. This is why it fixes and loses problems at the rate of a fresh sample, and why voting (which averages slips out) helps the base much more than RL.

explains.quote: Truncating the tail at T 1.0 brings loops back
explains.how: The same tail tokens cause the slips and break the loops, so cutting the tail at T 1.0 trades slips for loops.
Every truncation rule removes slips and adds loops at about equal cost, so none clears 420.
RL puts little mass in the tail, so raising T from 0.6 to 1.0 draws few extra derailing tokens.

explains.quote: D follows the answer format, not correctness
explains.how: Errors build up over many positions instead of starting at one decisive token, so the answer-start hypothesis fails.

explains.quote: the top 4 % of positions carry 38.7 % of KL
explains.how: A small tail shrink at every position spreads the KL out instead of concentrating it on a few forking tokens.
The tail shrink acts at every position, so the lens difference does not peak at the first wrong step.

explains.quote: no J-lens feature predicts a wrong base answer better than length
explains.how: When each position carries a similar slip risk, the number of positions (length) is the best single predictor of error.

explains.quote: H1 and H2 of specs/SPEC_day1_length_rules.md refuted
explains.how: Cutoffs on length do not change the per-token slip rate, so picking or restarting by length cannot remove the errors.

explains.quote: gets 42 of the cued base's 90 wrong problems right
explains.how: Most base errors are random slips, so a fresh draw (the random cell) avoids nearly half of them.

explains.quote: RL stays 5.6 points ahead under the vote
explains.how: A vote averages out independent slips but does not remove errors that come back on every sample of a problem, so some of RL's lead survives.
Removing top-p at T 0.6 brings back only a little loop-breaking tail, so the effect is small and not significant.

conflicts.quote: a=0.25 is +6.2 pts over base cue [3.0, 9.6], later steps flat
conflicts.how: A tail shrink that scaled with dose should keep improving after a = 0.25. The flat curve needs the tail to saturate early, which the theory does not derive.
Cap hits without a loop are failures to stop, not slips, so this share of the gap is outside the mechanism.

rival: The strongest rival is that RL teaches a stopping and commitment policy (when to settle and finish) and leaves the content tokens as they are. That rival predicts the same tail mass per token for RL's own text and the base's own text, and no gap in per-token log-prob between right and wrong finished base answers. This theory predicts RL has clearly less tail and higher per-token entropy loss in wrong base answers. The per-position tail-rate ratio and the entropy ratio below separate the two.

predictions.experiment: Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math, plain prompt, MATH-500 n = 500, T 1.3 / top-p 1.0 / no min-p, cap 16,384, one sample, seed base 45,000,000, grader v3, on one H100.
predictions.refuted_by: Fewer than 432 right: RL's tail would not be shrunk enough to make it robust above T 1.0.

predictions.experiment: Base Olmo-3-1025-7B with the cue, MATH-500 n = 500, T 1.3 / top-p 1.0 / no min-p, cap 16,384, one sample, seed base 41,000,000, grader v3, on one H100.
predictions.refuted_by: 396 or more right (the base as temperature-robust as RL, within 15 points of its T 1.0 score of 410), or fewer than 280.

predictions.experiment: Offline: per-token entropy of each model on its own answers at T 1.0, RL plain (T2) against cued base (T1).
predictions.recipe: File studies/rlneurons/results/rln5/map-01/checks.json, key per_row, lists T1 and T2 (500 rows each, no filter). For each row compute h = sum_entropy_own / n_own and skip rows with n_own = 0. Take the mean of h over the T2 rows and the mean of h over the T1 rows, then report ratio = mean_T2 / mean_T1. Cap hits are kept as they are.
predictions.unit: ratio of mean per-token entropy (RL own / base own)
predictions.refuted_by: A ratio above 0.80: RL's per-token distribution would not be clearly sharper than the base's on its own text.

predictions.experiment: Offline: does per-token surprisal pick out wrong finished base answers at T 1.0?
predictions.recipe: Join studies/rlneurons/results/rln5/map-01/checks.json per_row list T1 with studies/rlneurons/results/rln4/t1_t2_items-01/per_problem.json on problem_index. Keep rows with t1_cap_hit false and n_own > 0. Score s = -sum_logprob_own / n_own (mean negative log-prob per generated token under the base) and label = 1 if t1_right is false. Report the AUROC of s for label 1 against label 0, using the Mann-Whitney statistic with ties counted as 0.5.
predictions.refuted_by: An AUROC below 0.58: wrong finished base answers would not hold more improbable tokens per position.

predictions.experiment: Offline: per-position tail rate, RL on its own text against the base on its own text.
predictions.recipe: Per-position shards on Modal Volume iterate-runs:sameraslan-1114-135831-c3ec/ (fields listed in the jobs/rln5_map.py docstring). For the 500 T1 answers, count the generated positions after the cue where the written token's log-prob under the base is below ln(0.01) = -4.6052, and divide by the total number of T1 generated positions after the cue (pooled rate). For the 500 T2 answers, count the positions where the written token's log-prob under RL is below -4.6052, divided by the total number of T2 generated positions (pooled rate). Report rate_T2 / rate_T1. All answers are kept, cap hits included.
predictions.unit: ratio of pooled tail-token rates (RL/T2 over base/T1)
predictions.refuted_by: A ratio above 0.75: RL draws tail tokens about as often as the base, so the tail-shrink mechanism fails.
